items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:1
items.html:
Circles and Straightness, comprising ten chapters

Chapter One
Explains: the ten Sefirot of the circles. And it contains six matters: A. The circles are the aspect of GaR. B. In the Sefirot of the circles, the more external is the more important. And the reverse is so in the Sefirot of straightness, where the more internal is the more important. C. Two aspects of reception in the vessels: 1. Through their internality. 2. Through their externality. D. Phase four cannot be revealed except through the three phases that precede it, which cause its revelation. E. The four phases are like four shells lying one atop another in the wall of a vessel, where the abundance is received in the innermost shell. F. Every screen that is thicker raises reflected light to a higher degree, and there are five degrees.

The circles are the aspect of GaR.
Now, concerning the ten Sefirot of the circles, the Rav spoke very little, and even these few words seem, at first glance, to be full of contradictions. However, it is impossible to expand on them at length, because they are the aspect of the first three Sefirot, which we are forbidden to engage with. Yet those few things the Rav wrote must be explained at least with a broad and clear explanation, in a manner sufficient for the purpose the Rav intended by them — namely, to the extent necessarily required for the connections of wisdom.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:2
items.html:
In the Sefirot of the circles, the more external is the more important
Let us first understand the matter in general, for the Rav divides the whole of reality by two discernments, namely: circles and straightness. That is, all the Partzufim found in the five worlds — Adam Kadmon and ABYA, down to this world — each contains an aspect of ten Sefirot of the circles and ten Sefirot of straightness. Now, we have seen that in the Sefirot of the circles, it is found that the more external something is, the more excellent it is, and the more internal something is, the more inferior it is. For the uppermost circle, which is closest to the Ein Sof that surrounds and encompasses the whole of reality, is the most excellent of all and is called Keter. Within it is the second circle, called Hochma, which is inferior to Keter, and so on, down to the innermost sphere of all, which is this world — the most inferior of all the circles, being darkness without light and full of filth. Thus, every more internal circle is more inferior, and every more external circle is more excellent.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:3
items.html:
In the Sefirot of straightness, the more internal is the more important
The Sefirot of straightness are the reverse, for in them, the more internal something is, the more praiseworthy it is. For the ten Sefirot of straightness that are the first and most internal of all are the ten Sefirot of the world of Adam Kadmon, called the line that expands from Ein Sof, extending close to this world without touching it. Upon its externality are clothed the ten Sefirot of straightness of the second world, called the world of Atzilut, whose level descends from the world of Adam Kadmon. And upon the externality of the world of Atzilut are clothed the ten Sefirot of straightness of the world of Beria, which is inferior to Atzilut, and so on, down to the ten Sefirot of straightness of the world of Assiya, which is the most inferior of all, clothing the externality of all the worlds together. Thus, in the Sefirot of straightness, it is found that each one is more inferior than the one it clothes externally, while the more internal one is more excellent than the other — that is, the reverse of the ten Sefirot of the circles, as above. Indeed, a great and profound matter lies in this opposition between the Sefirot of the circles and the Sefirot of straightness, and it must be well understood.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:4
items.html:
Two ways of reception in the vessel: 1) Through its innerness. 2) Through its externality.
You already know the matter of the middle point in Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, in which the restriction took place, whereby the light withdrew from around that point and an empty vacuum was made. (See above, Part One, Chapter One, Item 50, beginning "And behold, phase.") It was explained there that it is therefore called the "middle point," to indicate that it does not receive through its internality and innerness, but only through its externality, from its surroundings — for this reason it receives the light without measure or limit, since what receives from its externality sets no boundary on the light; see there. Thus we have two aspects of reception in vessels: one aspect is that which receives through its externality, and the second aspect is that which receives through its internality. Now, it is certain that what is meant here is not a matter of place and area, by which internality and externality would be pictured to you; hence, we must understand well what internality and externality we are dealing with here.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:5
items.html:
The first three phases are only causes for the revelation of Phase Four, and are not themselves receivers. Like four shells in the wall of a vessel.
Now, the spiritual vessel — you already know that its matter is the aspect of the "will" that is in the emanated being, to receive its abundance from Ein Sof. (See Introduction to the Book of the Ten Sefirot, Part One, Item 25.) You also know that in this will there are four phases, one below the other. That is, this vessel, namely the aforesaid "will to receive," is not fixed in the emanated being so as to be fit for its function until four phases pass over it by way of gradation: the first phase is a very faint will; Phase Two is greater than Phase One, and so on, up to Phase Four, which is the fullness of the will to the degree required for the final fixing of the vessel. The reason for this was already explained above (Part One, page 5, Chapter One, Item 50, beginning "And the reason," see there), because this will to receive is a form the very opposite, from one extreme to the other, of the will to bestow included in the light of Ein Sof, Blessed Be He. Hence it cannot be revealed all at once, but only gradually, beginning from the will to bestow included in the root, called Keter, and then to what is coarser than it, meaning somewhat different from it, which is Phase One, and then to what is still coarser, called Phase Two, and so on, up to Phase Four, which differs from the form of the light from one extreme to the other, and is therefore uniquely fit to serve the emanated being as a vessel. Whereas in the three preceding phases, the will to receive is not revealed in them to the degree required for the aspect of a vessel of reception. Therefore only Phase Four is considered the essential vessel of reception of the emanated being, and is for this reason called the aspect of the internality and innerness of the emanated being. Phase Three of the will, however, is considered to be external to Phase Four; Phase Two external to Phase Three; Phase One external to Phase Two; and the aspect of Keter is external to them all. This is similar to the wall of a physical vessel, made of four shells, one atop another, where the abundance received in that vessel is certainly found only in the innermost, fourth shell, while the three outer shells surrounding it are made there only for the purpose of strengthening that innermost, fourth shell. Judge likewise here: the light is received only in Phase Four, and the three phases preceding it are external to it, and exist only because Phase Four cannot be revealed except through a gradual unfolding, as explained above.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:6
items.html:
Internality and coarseness are one and the same. Externality and purity are one and the same.
Now it has been well explained to you, the internality and externality that must be discerned in every vessel. For since there are necessarily four phases in every vessel, as is known, the last phase among them is called the innerness and internality of that vessel, being the essential aspect of reception found in the vessel, while the phases that preceded it, in order to reveal the last phase, are considered the externality of the vessel. And every degree further from the last phase is considered more external. You also know that Phase One is purer than Phase Two, and Phase Four is the coarsest of all. Hence internality and coarseness are one and the same, and the fact that Phase Four is considered the phase that receives the abundance is only because it is the coarsest. And externality and purity are one and the same, because its will is faint and pure and closer to the aspect of the Emanator; therefore it is the most external, meaning it is furthest from being the aspect of reception, which is innerness and internality.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:7
items.html:
Closeness to, and distance from, the Emanator is measured according to the degree of reception in the emanated being.
This is what the Rav wrote regarding the Sefirot of the circles, that the more external something is, the more excellent it is and the closer it is to the Emanator. For the aspect of the root, called Keter, is the purest of all, and its form is closest to Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, more than all the rest; this is called being close to the Emanator, and this same fact is called being the most external of all — meaning it is very far from the aspect of innerness and internality, that is, from the aspect of reception, as above. After it comes Phase One, which is more internal than Keter, meaning closer to the aspect of reception than it. And Phase Two is more internal than it, meaning closer to Phase Four, which is the aspect of reception — until Phase Four, which is the true internality, meaning that the abundance is received in it, and therefore its form is furthest from the Emanator of them all, as above.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 1:8
items.html:
In the Sefirot of straightness, the measure of its stature depends on the reflected light that rises from the coarseness in the screen — the coarser it is, the greater its reflected light.
In the Sefirot of straightness, however, there is the matter of reflected light that rises from the coupling of the screen with the upper light (see Introduction to the Book of the Ten Sefirot, Part One, under the word "screen"). The measure of the greatness of this reflected light is measured by the degree of coarseness present in the screen that couples with the upper light. Where the screen is coarsest, namely Phase Four, it is found to reveal a complete stature of ten Sefirot, reaching up to Keter. But if the degree of coarseness in the screen is one phase less, containing only Phase Three, it is found to reveal only ten Sefirot each of which has no more than the stature of Hochma, lacking Keter. And if it contains only the coarseness of Phase Two, it is found to reveal only ten Sefirot each of which has no more than the stature of Bina, lacking Keter and lacking Hochma. And if the screen contains only the coarseness of Phase One, it is found to reveal ten Sefirot each of which has no more than the stature of Zeir Anpin. And if the screen is pure, without even the coarseness of Phase One, then it reveals no stature at all, only the aspect of Malchut alone. The reason for this will be explained in Part Three, God willing.
